close_reason: Added now_utc_string_checked() -> Option<UTCDate> as the typed-fallible variant. now_utc_string now delegates to it and .expects on None — converts silent sentinel propagation into a panic at the call site. dispatcher task::spawn isolation already converts handler panics to serverFail. All 30+ consumer call sites compile unchanged. Workspace cargo test + clippy pass. Tests: happy-path Some + cross-variant wire-format agreement.
description:
crate-jmap-server/src/helpers.rs:159-198 — now_utc_string returns UTCDate but on three distinct "this should never happen on a sane clock" branches returns the literal UTCDate::from("clock-out-of-range"):

  // u64 seconds exceeds i64::MAX — corrupted clock sentinel.
  Err(_) => return UTCDate::from("clock-out-of-range"),
  ...
  Some(neg) => (neg, d.subsec_millis()),
  None => return UTCDate::from("clock-out-of-range"),
  ...
  Err(_) => return UTCDate::from("clock-out-of-range"),

A serious Rust practitioner reads this and winces. The function's public contract says it returns a UTCDate — a typed wire-format wrapper — but on the failure branch the wrapper holds a 19-byte ASCII sentinel that:

  1. Is not a valid wire-format timestamp (would fail any UTCDate::new_validated check, and even fail the looser 24-char shape check the function's own docs acknowledge).
  2. Has no in-band signal that distinguishes it from a real timestamp. Downstream code that interpolates the value into a JSON response or a log line emits "clock-out-of-range" verbatim, with no opportunity for the caller to react.
  3. Couples every downstream consumer that compares timestamps (database TTL, retention sweep, sort key) to a string-equality check against a magic literal nobody documented.

The idiomatic Rust shape for "operation may fail in a way the caller might want to handle" is Result or Option. Either:

  fn now_utc_string() -> Result<UTCDate, ClockError>

or (when the only sane response really is "give up"):

  fn now_utc_string() -> Option<UTCDate>

If the workspace decision is that callers cannot reasonably react to a clock fault — defensible — then the function should panic, not silently return a sentinel. A panic surfaces immediately at the call site and the operator can read the stack trace; a sentinel propagates through serialization, persistence, and downstream comparisons until someone notices a database row with the literal "clock-out-of-range" in a UTCDate column.

The sentinel-string pattern is also what motivated the typed-error / Result-shaped UTCDate work elsewhere in the workspace (UTCDate::new_validated). Keeping a magic-string failure mode on the producer side undoes that discipline.

What goes wrong if it stays as-is: silent propagation of a malformed UTCDate into any field that uses now_utc_string() as a default, including audit-log timestamps, last-seen markers, and message receivedAt fields. Operators with corrupted clocks (a not-uncommon failure mode on cheap VMs and unsynchronized embedded boxes) see "clock-out-of-range" land in their databases with no log warning. By the time anyone notices, the wire-format invariant is gone from a year of historical rows.

Recommended shape:

  fn now_utc_string() -> UTCDate {
      now_utc_string_checked().expect("system clock is reasonable")
  }

  fn now_utc_string_checked() -> Option<UTCDate> { ... }

or go the whole way to Result with a typed ClockError. Either path makes the failure mode addressable by callers that care (long-running daemons) and crash-loudly for those that don't (one-shot tools).

Related but distinct from JMAP-jfia.23 (UTCDate newtype invariant breach on the success path — the 24-char-with-millis output) and JMAP-jfia.11 (P4 dense pre-epoch ladder readability). Those are about the happy path; this is about the failure-mode shape.
title: now_utc_string returns sentinel String 'clock-out-of-range' instead of Result/Option
